entry: Greek god of blacksmiths, metalworking, and fire. In myth he was the son of [[Hera]], either alone or by [[Zeus]]. He was cast off [[Mount Olympus]] because of his lameness, either by his mother Hera or, in another account, by Zeus. As the smith of the gods, he made their weapons. He was worshipped in manufacturing centers, particularly in [[Athens]], and his cult was based on Lemnos. His symbols were the smith's hammer, anvil, and tongs, and the Romans equated him with Vulcan.

Greek goddess of marriage, women, and family, and protector of women in childbirth. She was queen of the [[Twelve Olympians|twelve Olympians]] on [[Mount Olympus]], sister and wife of [[Zeus]], and daughter of the [[Titans]] Cronus and Rhea. In myth she was jealous and vengeful toward Zeus's lovers and illegitimate children, and she persecuted the hero [[Heracles]]. In Hesiod's *Theogony* she bore [[Hephaestus]] alone, out of revenge for Zeus having fathered Athena without her. Her iconography shows a dignified, matronly figure, often crowned with a polos or diadem. Her sacred animals were the cow, cuckoo, and peacock, and she is sometimes shown holding a [[Pomegranate|pomegranate]] as an emblem of immortality. Her Roman counterpart was Juno. Her name appears on Linear B tablets from Pylos and Thebes but has no clear etymology. She was the tutelary goddess of Argos.

Greek hero, considered the greatest of the Greek heroes and both a hero and a god. He was regarded as the son of [[Zeus]] and Alcmene and was known for superhuman strength. Driven mad by the enmity of [[Hera]], he killed his wife Megara and their children. He then performed twelve labours for Eurystheus, king of Argos, including killing the Nemean lion and the Lernaean Hydra and capturing [[Cerberus]]. Other exploits included sailing with the Argonauts, sacking [[Troy]] before the [[Trojan War]], and freeing [[Prometheus]]. His wife Deianira, deceived by the dying centaur Nessus, gave him a garment smeared with poisoned blood. He immolated himself on Mount Oeta, burning away his mortal part, and ascended to Olympus as a god. Known to the Romans as Hercules, he was widely worshipped as a patron of young men and gymnasia, and Roman emperors such as [[Commodus]] identified themselves with him.

Pre-Socratic Greek philosopher from the port city of [[Ephesus]] in Ionia. He flourished around 500 BC and wrote a single work, of which only fragments survive. His paradoxical, oracular style earned him the epithets "the dark" and "the obscure". He became known as "the weeping philosopher", in contrast to [[Democritus]], "the laughing philosopher." His central ideas were the unity of opposites and constant change, expressed in sayings such as "Everything flows." He held that fire was the arche, or fundamental element, and that the logos gave structure to the world. His thought influenced [[Plato]], [[Aristotle]], the Stoics, and later [[Friedrich Nietzsche|Nietzsche]] and [[Martin Heidegger|Heidegger]].

Byzantine emperor (r. 610–641). He rose to power in 608, when he and his father, Heraclius the Elder, led a revolt against the unpopular emperor Phocas. His reign was dominated by war with the [[Sasanian Empire]]. Persian forces took Syria and Egypt, but Heraclius drove them out of Asia Minor and defeated them at Nineveh in 627. Khosrow II was overthrown by his son Kavad II, who sued for peace and agreed to withdraw from occupied territory. Heraclius soon lost many regained lands to the [[Rashidun Caliphate]], and in 636 the Arabs defeated his brother Theodore in Syria. His military reforms helped his successors resist the Arabs. He tried to repair the [[Schism|schism]] in the Christian church by promoting monothelitism, a compromise rejected by all sides. During his reign Greek replaced [[Latin]] as the official language of the state.

Discipline concerned with the design, display, and study of armorial bearings. A full heraldic achievement may include a coat of arms on a [[Shield|shield]], a helmet and crest, and supporters, badges, banners, and mottoes, formally described in a blazon. Devices signifying individuals and groups date back to antiquity, but regular hereditary designs did not develop until the [[Middle Ages|High Middle Ages]]. Early emblems, such as Egyptian royal symbols topped by the falcon of [[Horus]], are regarded as precursors, since no distinct symbolic language existed. Heraldry survived the abandonment of armour on the battlefield during the seventeenth century and is still used by individuals, organizations, and cities to symbolize heritage and aspirations. Related disciplines include vexillology, [[Genealogy|genealogy]], and the study of ceremony and rank. Heraldry has been described as the "handmaid of history."

City in western [[Afghanistan]], capital of Herat Province. It is the largest city in its province and the third-largest in the country. As the gateway to [[Iran]] and Turkmenistan, it collects large customs revenue. Herat lies in the fertile valley of the Hari River, south of the Paropamisus Mountains. An ancient city on the [[Silk Road]], it was traditionally known for its wine. In the Middle Ages it was called the Pearl of [[Khorasan]], and after its conquest by [[Timur]] it became a center of intellectual and artistic life. Under Shah Rukh and Husayn Bayqara it was the focus of the [[Timurid Empire|Timurid]] Renaissance. It remained part of [[Safavid Iran]] until the early 18th century, was later governed by Pashtun tribes, and was incorporated into Afghanistan in 1863. In 2021 it was announced that Herat would be listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Since August 2021 it has been under [[Taliban]] administration.

Savory or aromatic plant, excluding vegetables, used for flavoring food, for medicine, or for fragrance. Culinary use distinguishes herbs from [[Spice|spices]], which are usually dried and made from seeds, bark, roots, or fruits, whereas herbs are the leafy or flowering parts. In [[Botany|botany]], an herb is a plant without a woody stem whose aerial parts die back each season, and the adjective "herbaceous" derives from Latin for "grassy." Under this strict definition, sage, [[Rosemary|rosemary]], and lavender would be excluded because they have woody stems. Theophrastus divided the plant world into trees, shrubs, and herbs. The [[Talmud]] refers to approximately fifteen herbs used for seasoning. Herbs were grouped as pot herbs, sweet herbs such as [[Thyme|thyme]], and salad herbs. In the seventeenth century, selective breeding changed pot herbs so much that they came to be called [[Vegetable|vegetables]].

Study and use of medicinal plants, which are a basis of traditional medicine, also called herbalism or phytotherapy. Scientific evidence for many herbal treatments remains limited, and standards for purity or dosage are generally not provided. Herbal medicine has been used since at least the [[Paleolithic]] era, and written records survive from [[Sumer]], [[Egypt]], Greece, China, and India. The Ebers papyrus, dating from about 1550 BCE, covers more than 700 compounds. The [[World Health Organization|World Health Organization]] estimates that 80 percent of the population of some Asian and African countries uses herbal medicine for some aspect of primary health care. Some [[Prescription drug|prescription drugs]], including artemisinin, digoxin, quinine, and taxanes, have a basis in herbal remedies. In 2015 an Australian government review found no clear evidence of effectiveness for herbalism, one of 17 topics evaluated. Paraherbalism is the pseudoscientific use of plant or animal extracts as medicine.

American engineer and [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] politician, 31st [[President of the United States|president of the United States]] (1929–1933). One of the first graduates of [[Stanford University]], he became a wealthy mining engineer. During [[World War I]] he organized relief for Belgium, and President [[Woodrow Wilson]] later put him in charge of the Food Administration. As Secretary of Commerce he was influential in the development of air travel and radio. His presidency was dominated by the [[Great Depression]], and his response was widely seen as inadequate. He lost the 1932 election to [[Franklin D. Roosevelt]]. Historians generally rank him among the worst American presidents, though he was effective as a humanitarian and administrator.

English [[Polymath|polymath]] and philosopher. Although the phrase "survival of the fittest" strongly suggests natural selection, Spencer coined it in *Principles of Biology* (1864) after reading [[Charles Darwin|Darwin]]'s 1859 book *On the Origin of Species*. He also supported [[Jean-Baptiste Lamarck|Lamarckism]] and saw evolution as extending into sociology and ethics. He developed an all-embracing conception of evolution as the progressive development of the physical world, biological organisms, the human mind, and human societies. He wrote on ethics, religion, anthropology, economics, political theory, and psychology. In *Social Statics* (1851) he predicted that humanity would adapt to society until the state withered away. He disagreed with [[Auguste Comte|Comte]]'s [[Positivism|positivism]]. Spencer was highly influential during his lifetime, but his influence declined after 1900, when [[Talcott Parsons]] asked, "Who now reads Spencer?"

Austrian conductor, principal conductor of the Berlin Philharmonic for 34 years. Born Heribert Adolf Ernst Karajan in [[Salzburg]], he was of Greek ancestry and studied at the Mozarteum and the Vienna Academy. He made his conducting debut in Salzburg in 1929. While a [[Nazi Party|Nazi Party]] member, he conducted at the Berlin State Opera during [[World War II]], and his membership remained controversial throughout his career. Generally regarded as one of the greatest conductors of the 20th century, he was a dominant figure in European classical music from the mid-1950s until his death. He made a large number of recordings, and by one estimate he sold 200 million records.

Animal anatomically or physiologically adapted to feed mainly on plants, especially on vascular tissues such as foliage, fruits, and seeds. Herbivores typically have jaws or mouthparts that break plant material down mechanically, and digestive [[Enzyme|enzymes]] that break down polysaccharides. Grazing [[Horse|horses]] and [[Cattle|cattle]] have wide, flat-crowned teeth for grinding grass and tree bark, and many evolved rumination or cecotropic behavior to extract more nutrients. Many herbivores also host gut bacteria and [[Protozoa|protozoa]] that degrade [[Cellulose|cellulose]], which is harder to digest than the protein- and fat-rich tissues eaten by [[Carnivore|carnivores]]. The term derives from Latin *herba* and *vorare*, "to devour," and was cited by [[Charles Lyell]] in his 1830 *Principles of Geology*. Fossils show that arthropods were feeding on plants less than 20 million years after the first land plants evolved.

Social group of animals of the same species, usually mammals, most particularly grazing [[Ungulate|ungulates]]. Herds, whether wild or domestic, tend to act together without planning or coordination, each individual responding to the others or to the same external circumstances. The collective behavior is called herding, and the animals are gregarious. Birds form flocks, and large groups of carnivores are called packs, though herd is used generically in theoretical discussions of [[Ecology|behavioral ecology]]. The most studied benefit is the dilution effect: an individual's risk of being preyed upon is smaller in a larger group, because a predator must choose which animal to attack. Some herds have control animals whose behavior predicts that of the whole herd. The word can also refer to people who tend domesticated animals, such as shepherds, goatherds, and cowherds.

Dog trained to herd [[Livestock|livestock]], or a breed developed for herding. Also called a stock dog or working dog, it is a sheepdog if trained for [[Sheep|sheep]] and a cattle dog if trained for [[Cattle|cattle]]. Herding dogs developed alongside the breeding of sheep, goats, and cattle. Sheep and goats were first domesticated in Western Asia, in the territory of modern Iran and Iraq. The early task of herding dogs was to protect herds from wild predators, which required strength and courage. Joint remains of sheep and dogs date to 3685 BC. Writings by [[Cato the Elder]] and Varro describe dogs used to guard herds and for military purposes. As large predators disappeared from much of [[Europe]], herding dogs protected crops and moved herds, and most Central European shepherd breeds took form in the 16th and 17th centuries. The Chiribaya culture of [[Peru]] and [[Chile]] bred herding dogs to manage llamas.

British breed of beef cattle from Herefordshire, England. It was developed through [[Selective breeding|selective breeding]] from the mid-eighteenth century by a few Herefordshire families, and the white face characteristic of the modern breed was well established by the end of the 18th century. In 2023, 62 countries reported populations totalling over seven million head, with more than 100,000 in Uruguay, Brazil, and Chile. Herefords reached Ireland in 1775 and [[Kentucky]] in 1817, and the modern American Hereford derives from a herd established in 1840 in [[Albany, New York]]. A hornless variant, the Polled Hereford, arose through a [[Gene|polled gene]] and was selected into a separate breed from 1889. Eye cancer occurs in Herefords, notably in countries with bright sunlight, and [[Dwarfism|dwarfism]] is caused by an autosomal recessive gene.

Belief or theory strongly at variance with established beliefs or customs, especially the accepted religious law of a religious organization. A heretic is a proponent of a heresy, and the study of heresy is called heresiology. Heresy differs from [[Apostasy|apostasy]], the explicit renunciation of one's religion, and from blasphemy. In Judaism, Christianity, and Islam, heresy has been met with censure ranging from excommunication to death. The word comes from Greek *haíresis*, originally meaning "choice." [[Irenaeus]] gave the term wide currency in his 2nd-century tract *Against Heresies*, using it against the [[Gnosticism|Gnostics]]. To end the doctrinal debate started by [[Arius]], [[Constantine the Great]] called the first ecumenical councils and enforced orthodoxy by imperial authority. In AD 380 the Edict of Thessalonica of [[Theodosius I]] first used the term in a legal context. Priscillian, the first Christian heretic to be executed, was condemned for sorcery in 386.

Belgian cartoonist, creator of *The Adventures of Tintin*. Born Georges Prosper Remi in Etterbeek, [[Brussels]], he took the pen name Hergé from the French pronunciation of his reversed initials, RG. He began as an illustrator for [[Scouting|scouting]] magazines before creating *The Adventures of Tintin* in 1929 for the conservative Catholic newspaper *Le Vingtième Siècle*. The early volumes were conservative propaganda for children, but from 1934 he researched his stories more carefully, which increased their realism. His clear-line style, known as *ligne claire*, was influential. During the German occupation he continued the series in *Le Soir*, a newspaper controlled by the [[Nazism|Nazi]] administration. After the liberation he was accused of collaboration, but no charges were brought against him. In 1946 he founded *Tintin* magazine with Raymond Leblanc, and in 1950 he established Studios Hergé. A Hergé Museum was established in Louvain-la-Neuve in 2009.

American novelist and poet of the American Renaissance. Born in New York City, he went to sea in 1839, and in 1841 he sailed on the whaler *Acushnet*, jumping ship in the Marquesas Islands. His first books, *Typee* (1846) and *Omoo* (1847), drew on his encounters with the peoples of [[Polynesia]]. Their success allowed him to marry Elizabeth Shaw, the daughter of a [[Boston]] jurist. His ambitious novel *Moby-Dick* (1851) found little audience in his lifetime. After moving to New York City in 1863, he worked as a United States customs inspector and turned to poetry. His poetic reflection on the moral questions of the [[American Civil War]], *Battle-Pieces and Aspects of the War* (1866), was followed by the epic *Clarel* (1876). His novella *Billy Budd, Sailor* was left unfinished and published posthumously in 1924. *Moby-Dick* is now considered one of the Great American Novels.

German [[Nazi Party|Nazi]] politician and Luftwaffe commander. A World War I fighter ace awarded the Pour le Mérite, he was wounded in the [[Beer Hall Putsch]] of 1923 and became addicted to morphine while being treated. After [[Adolf Hitler|Hitler]] became chancellor, Göring oversaw the creation of the [[Gestapo]], which he handed to [[Heinrich Himmler|Himmler]] in 1934. From 1936 he led the Four Year Plan to mobilize the economy for war. He was named Hitler's successor in 1939. His standing declined as the Luftwaffe failed to prevent Allied bombing of Germany. He acquired property and artwork, much of it stolen from Jewish victims of the [[The Holocaust|Holocaust]]. In April 1945, after he asked Hitler's permission to take over the Reich, Hitler removed him from all positions. Convicted at the [[Nuremberg trials]] in 1946, he was sentenced to hang, but took his own life with cyanide the night before his scheduled execution.

German-Swiss poet and novelist, winner of the 1946 Nobel Prize in Literature. He was born in the [[Black Forest]] town of Calw, in Württemberg, into a Pietist family with links to the [[Basel|Basel]] Mission in India. His interest in Eastern religions and in Jungian analysis shaped his work. His best-known novels, including *Demian*, *Siddhartha*, *Steppenwolf*, *Narcissus and Goldmund*, and *The Glass Bead Game*, explore the search for authenticity, self-knowledge, and [[Spirituality|spirituality]]. He was widely read in German-speaking countries during his lifetime, but his international fame came in the mid-1960s, when post-war readers in the United States and Europe embraced his works. He settled permanently in Switzerland from 1904.

German mathematician, theoretical physicist, logician, and philosopher. He earned his doctorate at the [[University of Göttingen]] under [[David Hilbert]] and became a professor in [[Zurich|Zürich]] in 1913. There he overlapped with [[Albert Einstein]], and he was one of the first to combine general relativity with electromagnetism. He originated [[Gauge theory|gauge theory]], developing the concept of gauge invariance, and pioneered the application of [[Group theory|group theory]] to [[Quantum mechanics|quantum mechanics]]. His foundational contributions extended to differential geometry and number theory, with results including the Peter–Weyl theorem and the Weyl law. In cosmology he theoretically derived a linear redshift–distance relation several years before Hubble's observations. As an important member of the Institute for Advanced Study in its early years, he conceived of mathematics as an organic whole.

German physicist and physician. He is remembered for linking theory with practical research. His work on the eye included theories of vision, the visual perception of space, and [[Color vision|color vision]], and he invented the ophthalmoscope in 1851. He is credited with the first formulation of the [[Conservation of energy|conservation of energy]] principle in its maximally general form, although credit is shared with Julius von Mayer, James Joule, and [[Daniel Bernoulli]]. In physics he also worked on electrodynamics, chemical thermodynamics, and hydrodynamic stability. As a philosopher he examined the relation between the laws of perception and the laws of nature, drawing on [[Immanuel Kant|Kant]]. He held chairs at Königsberg, Bonn, and Heidelberg before becoming professor of physics at the University of [[Berlin]] in 1871. The Helmholtz Association, the largest German association of research institutions, is named after him.

Olympian deity in Greek religion and mythology, considered the herald of the gods. He was also the protector of heralds, travelers, thieves, merchants, and orators, and a psychopomp who guided souls into the afterlife. Often presented as the son of [[Zeus]] and Maia, he is known as the "divine trickster," and the Homeric Hymn to Hermes gives the best-known account of his cunning. He moved freely between the mortal and divine worlds on winged sandals. His attributes include the herma, rooster, tortoise, satchel, and winged helmet, and his main symbol is the caduceus, a winged staff entwined with two snakes. The Romans identified many of his traits with Mercury, a name derived from Latin *merx*, "merchandise," which is the origin of the words "merchant" and "[[Commerce|commerce]]." The name is attested in Mycenaean Greek as e-ma-a2 on Linear B tablets.

Philosophical and religious tradition based on writings attributed to Hermes Trismegistus, a figure combining the Greek Hermes and the Egyptian [[Thoth]]. The religio-philosophical Hermetica, written in Egypt from about 100 to 300 CE, include the *Corpus Hermeticum*, a collection of seventeen Greek treatises. In the [[Renaissance]], Marsilio Ficino's translation of these texts inspired a movement that also drew on [[Alchemy|alchemy]] and astrology. Alchemy was often called the Hermetic art, and its role in the thought of [[Isaac Newton]] and [[Robert Boyle]] is now widely recognized. A generic, pseudo-historical sense of the term was popularized by nineteenth- and twentieth-century occultists.
